claims.text: The initially solid nanoparticles are single-phase Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu high-entropy alloys.
Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu HEA nanoparticles inherently contain atomic-scale compositional fluctuations.
Atomic-scale compositional fluctuations produce spatially heterogeneous bonding strengths.
Increasing a system from two to five elements reduces the concentration of each individual atom type.
Dilution of the constituent elements creates local regions with different bond strengths.
Regions having weaker local bonding have lower local critical melting temperatures.
Low-local-melting-temperature regions begin to melt before the rest of the HEA nanoparticle.
The sequential melting of chemically distinct local regions produces a diffuse, progressive melting transition.
Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu HEA nanoparticles will begin premelting at a lower temperature than size-matched single-metal or bimetallic nanoparticles.
Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu HEA nanoparticles will melt over a broader temperature interval than size-matched single-metal or bimetallic nanoparticles.
Comparable single-metal and bimetallic nanoparticles exhibit sharper melting transitions within narrower temperature windows.
The proposed mechanism is limited to homogeneous, single-phase HEA nanoparticles heated under inert conditions with tightly controlled size, heating rate, surface effects, and defect content.
Synthesis-induced defects may affect the melting behavior.
A melting transition as sharp and narrowly distributed as that of the baseline particles would falsify the proposed local-bonding-heterogeneity explanation.
